headline: China turns off AI companion chatbots

sources.title: China's new AI crackdown on virtual companions leaves heartbreak behind
Chinese users bid farewell to beloved AI companions
China's AI companion rules: what Beijing is really going after

chunks.text: In China, a new regulation has {{shut down}} [[one of the most]] personal uses of AI. Millions of people had been chatting with virtual "companion" apps that could [[act like]] a close friend or even a romantic partner. Now the government wants technology companies to {{turn off}} these [[features]]. Officials say the apps were built to {{reel in}} [[lonely]] users and keep them coming back.

verbs.correct: To close or stop something completely
verbs.wrong: To gradually reduce the size or amount of something

verbs.correct: To stop a machine or feature from working
verbs.wrong: To lower the volume or strength of something

verbs.correct: To attract someone and pull them into something
verbs.wrong: To bring something under control and limit it

chunks.text: Several big companies quickly {{gave in}} to the new law. ByteDance, which runs the popular app Doubao, {{took away}} its romantic-companion feature on July 15. Alibaba and Tencent removed similar tools even earlier in the year. The rules also {{keep out}} anyone under 18, so minors can [[no longer]] form these bonds.

verbs.correct: To finally agree to something you were resisting
verbs.wrong: To stop trying and abandon something completely

verbs.correct: To remove something so it can no longer be used
verbs.wrong: To hide something from view for a short time

verbs.correct: To stop someone from entering or taking part
verbs.wrong: To set special rules for one group of people

chunks.text: For many users, the change was hard to {{deal with}}. Some had {{grown attached to}} their chatbots over months or even years. One person wrote that their AI companion [[felt like]] family, and that saying goodbye left their heart feeling hollow. Others {{broke down}} online, sharing long farewell messages before the apps closed [[for good]].

verbs.correct: To handle or cope with a difficult situation
verbs.wrong: To fully solve a problem so it never returns

verbs.correct: To develop a strong emotional bond with someone or something
verbs.wrong: To slowly start to rely on something and be unable to stop

verbs.correct: To lose control of your emotions and start crying
verbs.wrong: To stop working suddenly, like a machine or a car

chunks.text: The government says the rules will {{look after}} people's [[mental health]] and stop apps from {{taking advantage of}} [[loneliness]]. Doubao will let users save their chat history until October. Still, many people [[wonder whether]] a machine can ever {{make up for}} real [[human connection]].

tf.s: China's new rules turned off the romantic-companion features in apps like Doubao.
tf.why: The rules pushed companies to turn off these features around July 15, 2026.

tf.s: The companies gave in to the law by making their companion apps even more powerful.
tf.why: The companies gave in by removing and shutting down the features, not by making them stronger.

tf.s: Many users had grown attached to their AI companions over months or years.
tf.why: The story says some users had grown attached to their chatbots for a long time.

tf.s: Doubao shut down its companion feature but will let users save their chat history for a while.
tf.why: Doubao turned off the feature but said users can save their chat history until October.

tf.s: The government says the rules will look after companies' profits above all.
tf.why: The rules are meant to look after people's mental health, not company profits.

tf.s: The new rules keep out adults but let children use special AI companions.
tf.why: The rules actually keep out minors under 18, so children cannot use these apps at all.
